strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: shifting from text-only world models for GUI/web agents to a visual world model that generates actual future GUI images, addressing a clear gap in the literature.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) idea is a clever and practical solution to the well-known difficulty of diffusion models rendering legible small text, decoupling layout/graphic generation (diffusion) from text content generation (LLM).

Comprehensive evaluation protocol spanning GUI quality (consistency, instructional accuracy, action readiness), trajectory synthesis, and downstream agent decision-making across multiple existing agents (T3A, M3A, APP-Agent, Mobile-Agent-v2) and multiple world-model baselines (language- and vision-based).
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (static text retention, action instructions vs. commands) that isolate the contribution of specific design choices.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix with prompts, dataset construction details, evaluation protocols, and additional qualitative visualizations including generalization to novel action-observation combinations.

Consistent, non-trivial performance gains over baselines across nearly all reported metrics and agents (e.g., ~29% relative improvement in GUI quality harmonic score, ~9-14% agent step-accuracy gains).
weaknesses: The evaluation dataset/test split is quite small (57 sampled episodes across 19 apps for main experiments), and while a full-split appendix result is mentioned, the core comparisons and case studies rely on a limited sample, raising concerns about statistical robustness and generalization to a broader app ecosystem.

The overall pipeline is computationally and architecturally heavy at inference time: for each candidate action the agent must run a diffusion-based STR predictor plus several sequential LLM calls (unchanged-symbol detection, semantic role assignment, text content prediction, action scoring, action selection). Latency/cost analysis and practicality for real-time agent deployment are not discussed.

The GUI-text predictor and STR extraction rely on hand-crafted heuristics (fixed BGR color thresholds for detecting black borders/white fill, contour-area ratio thresholds) that seem fragile to UI theme variation (e.g., dark mode, differently styled placeholders), and the paper's own failure-case figure (Fig. 11) shows this breaking down without deeper analysis of frequency/impact.

Key evaluation metrics (instructional accuracy, action readiness, trajectory correctness) are all LLM-as-judge based, with no human validation, inter-annotator agreement, or correlation analysis to establish their reliability.

Missing an important ablation: a version of the pipeline using a single end-to-end diffusion model to generate the full GUI (graphics+text) without STR decoupling would more directly quantify the benefit of the graphic/text decomposition versus just being a stronger/more specialized model relative to generic baselines like IP2P/UI-diffuser.

Baselines such as UI-diffuser and InstructPix2Pix are not originally designed for this exact conditional next-GUI-prediction task, making the comparison somewhat imbalanced in ViMo's favor; a more tailored, strong pixel-space baseline fine-tuned specifically for this task (beyond generic image editing models) would strengthen the claims.

The performance gains for the ultimate downstream metric (agent step accuracy) are relatively modest (~9-14% relative) given the substantial complexity and inference overhead added by the full ViMo pipeline, raising questions about the cost-benefit tradeoff in practice.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine practical problem: existing pixel-level image generation models produce distorted/illegible text in GUI screenshots, which is a real limitation for app-agent world models.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) idea of decoupling graphic generation (diffusion) from text-content generation (LLM) is a reasonably intuitive engineering solution to the text-rendering problem.

The paper evaluates the method across a fairly wide set of downstream settings: GUI quality, trajectory synthesis, and integration with 6 different existing App agents (language- and multi-modality-based), showing consistent (if modest) improvements.
Ablation studies on static-text preservation and action-instruction vs. action-command conditioning provide some evidence for specific design choices.
The paper includes many qualitative visualizations and a reasonably detailed appendix with prompts, which aids partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core system is a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion/InstructPix2Pix-style model combined with off-the-shelf OCR and heavy LLM prompting; none of the individual components are new, and the contribution is largely an engineering pipeline rather than a new modeling technique.

The multi-stage GUI-text predictor pipeline is fragile and heuristic-heavy: text-symbol detection relies on hand-tuned BGR color thresholds and contour-area ratios (Appendix A), and Fig. 11 shows clear failure cases where symbols are not correctly recognized, undermining claims of robustness.

Evaluation metrics (sgc, sia, sar) and the trajectory-matching judgments are computed via LLM-as-judge without any reported human validation or inter-rater agreement, raising concerns about reliability and potential bias favoring the proposed method's design.

The test set is very small and possibly non-representative: only 57 sampled episodes across 19 apps are used for most experiments (a "partial split" rather than full evaluation), and although a full-split comparison is given in the appendix (Table 9), it is limited to one metric family and not extended to the trajectory/agent experiments.

No analysis of inference cost/latency is provided, despite the pipeline requiring a diffusion forward pass plus multiple sequential LLM calls (static-text detection, semantic-role assignment, text-content prediction, and later two more LLM calls for action selection) — this could make real-time app-agent deployment impractical, which is not discussed.

Performance gains in the agent-enhanced setting are relatively modest in absolute terms (e.g., T3A 43.13→49.20, M3A 46.01→50.16), and the "29.14%" and "14.07%" relative-improvement figures in the abstract can overstate the practical significance of these differences.

Baselines are largely adapted from other domains (website world models converted to App setting, generic image-editing models like InstructPix2Pix) rather than strong, purpose-built competitors, making it unclear how ViMo would fare against more carefully designed vision-based GUI world model baselines.
The ablation study is narrow (only two design choices tested), leaving many architectural and pipeline choices (e.g., OCR model choice, LLM choice, color-based symbol detection) unvalidated.

The dataset construction (mixing Android Control and AITW, manual filtering of apps, GPT-4o-based action-instruction conversion) introduces multiple potential sources of noise and bias that are not rigorously quantified.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap: existing GUI world models are text-only and lack visual fidelity, while naive pixel-based image generation fails badly at text rendering (well illustrated in Fig. 2).

The core idea of Symbolic Text Representation (STR) — decoupling graphic generation (diffusion) from text content generation (LLM) — is a simple, well-motivated, and reasonably novel engineering solution to the text-in-image distortion problem.

The evaluation is broad: GUI quality metrics (consistency, instructional accuracy, action readiness), trajectory synthesis, and downstream integration with 6 different App agents (language- and multi-modality-based), showing consistent improvements over multiple baselines (HTML-vision, IP2P, UI-diffuser, Change-text, HTML-text).
Useful ablations isolate the contribution of static text preservation and action instructions vs. action commands, and a randomness check (3 runs) supports result stability.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: prompts, dataset construction details, category breakdowns, and many qualitative examples (including generalization to novel action-observation combinations) are provided in the appendix.
Practical significance: demonstrated relative gains (9-14%) in App agent step accuracy when using ViMo as an auxiliary world model, suggesting real utility for long-horizon planning tasks.
weaknesses: The dataset is small in scale (19 apps, 57 sampled test episodes, ~3550 episodes total) relative to the diversity of real-world mobile app ecosystems, raising concerns about generalization claims and statistical robustness of the reported gains.

Nearly all evaluation metrics (sia, sar, trajectory matching) rely on LLM-as-judge scoring with no human evaluation or human-agreement study, which could introduce systematic bias or inconsistency that isn't accounted for.

The GUI-text predictor pipeline involves multiple sequential LLM calls (unchanged-text detection, semantic role assignment, text content prediction) which adds latency/cost not discussed or benchmarked, limiting practical deployment insight.

The technical novelty of the STR predictor itself is limited — it is essentially a fine-tuned InstructPix2Pix/Stable Diffusion model conditioned on STR images; the main contribution is the data representation trick rather than a new generative architecture.

Failure cases (Fig. 11) show the text-symbol detection/generation pipeline is fragile in some cases, and the paper does not quantify how often such failures occur or their downstream impact on agent performance.

Baselines for 'world models' are adaptations of website-based methods to the App setting (Change-text, HTML-text/vision), which may not represent the strongest possible comparison points for App-specific world models, potentially inflating relative improvement numbers.
Limited discussion of computational cost/inference time compared to baselines, which is relevant for an agent-in-the-loop planning use case where multiple action outcomes must be simulated per step.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of decoupling graphic and text generation via the Symbolic Text Representation (STR), which directly addresses a real and demonstrated failure mode (pixel-level text distortion) of prior image-based GUI/world-model generation methods.

Comprehensive evaluation spanning three complementary axes: intrinsic world-model quality (automatic metrics + user study), downstream agent decision-making (multiple agents, multiple world-model baselines), and real-world applicability (zero-shot generalization to unseen apps, online navigation with AndroidWorld).

Strong and consistent empirical gains across many settings: improvements over IP2P*, UI-diffuser, HTML-vision/text, and Change-text baselines across several different App agents (T3A, M3A, APP-Agent, Mobile-Agent-v2), suggesting the benefit is not cherry-picked to one agent.

Reasonably thorough ablations (static text preservation, action instruction vs. command conditioning, iteration/rollout depth) and extra robustness checks (randomness across runs, full vs. sampled test split) that support the claimed design choices.
Practical considerations addressed, including inference time/hardware requirements and a discussion of misuse risk with proposed safeguards for release.
weaknesses: The dataset scale is quite small (19 apps, ~3,550 episodes) and evaluation for the main world-model quality benchmark is done on only 57 sampled episodes and 80 user-study samples, raising concerns about statistical robustness and generalization claims despite the added full-split/randomness check being limited in scope.

The GUI-text predictor pipeline is a complex, multi-stage handcrafted system (OCR detection, LLM-based static text filtering, symbol localization via hard-coded color/contour heuristics, multiple sequential LLM calls for role inference and text prediction, then heuristic overlay/font-sizing) which raises reproducibility and robustness concerns, especially given the acknowledged failure cases where symbols aren't correctly rendered (Fig. 6).

Reliance on GPT-4o/Gemini as both the text predictor and as the automatic LLM-based evaluator (sia, sar) creates potential circularity and self-evaluation bias in the automatic metrics; the user study helps but is based on a small, potentially non-expert crowd (70 volunteers) with unclear inter-rater reliability reporting.

The relative-improvement percentages emphasized in the abstract/intro (e.g., 182.74% user-study gain) are somewhat inflated framing given the low absolute baseline scores of compared methods (which were not originally designed for this exact task), potentially overstating the significance of the contribution.

Limited analysis of failure modes/error accumulation beyond a brief ablation; the STR representation's reliance on exact color/border matching for symbol detection seems brittle and its impact on downstream agent tasks in truly diverse, uncontrolled real apps is not deeply probed.

Baselines for GUI image generation (IP2P, UI-diffuser, TextDiffuser-2) are not originally designed for this exact next-GUI-prediction task, and while IP2P was fine-tuned (IP2P*), the comparison may still be somewhat unfair without more tailored adaptation of these baselines to the world-model setting.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: extending world models for GUI agents from purely textual descriptions to visual/pixel-level predictions, which is a reasonable and practically motivated direction.

The paper conducts a wide range of experiments -- automatic metrics, human user studies, downstream agent decision-making across 6 different App agents, online navigation on AndroidWorld, and zero-shot generalization to unseen apps -- giving a broad (if not always deep) picture of the method's behavior.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) idea, which masks text with placeholder boxes so that a diffusion model only needs to predict layout/graphics while an LLM fills in text content, is a sensible and interpretable engineering solution to the well-known failure of diffusion models to render legible text.
Reasonable ablations (static text preservation, action instruction vs. command conditioning, roll-out iterations) that attempt to justify individual design choices.
Practical considerations such as inference time and GPU memory requirements are reported, showing some awareness of deployability.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core pipeline is essentially (1) OCR-based text masking, (2) a fine-tuned InstructPix2Pix-style diffusion model for the masked layout, and (3) a multi-stage LLM prompting pipeline to reinsert text. Each component reuses fairly standard off-the-shelf techniques (OCR, IP2P fine-tuning, LLM-based text infill), and the overall decoupling of layout vs. text generation is conceptually similar to existing scene-text generation approaches (e.g., TextDiffuser-style two-stage layout-then-text pipelines) applied to a new domain rather than a fundamentally new modeling contribution.

The text-symbol localization procedure relies on brittle hand-crafted heuristics (fixed BGR color thresholds for black borders/white fills, contour-to-bounding-box area ratios) that are shown in the appendix (Fig. 6) to fail on diverse GUI themes (e.g., dark mode, colored buttons), raising concerns about robustness beyond the narrow set of evaluated apps/themes.

Small-scale, narrow evaluation: the dataset covers only 19 apps and, for the main GUI-quality evaluation, only 57 sampled episodes (a 'partial split') are used rather than the full test set, which limits confidence in the generality and statistical robustness of the reported gains; the randomness study only reports 3 runs with no confidence intervals in the main tables.

Automatic evaluation metrics (sia, sar) are LLM-as-judge scores, which are known to be susceptible to bias/inconsistency; while a user study is included, it is based on only 80 samples across 4 methods (20 per method) and 70 participants rating each on 3 questions, a fairly small sample for the claimed 'robust and holistic' assessment.

Baselines for the 'world model' comparisons (UI-diffuser, IP2P fine-tuned on GUI data, HTML-rendered-vision) are somewhat weak or ad hoc adaptations rather than strong, purpose-built competitors; no comparison is made against stronger recent multimodal/unified generative models that might already handle text-in-image rendering better, which weakens claims of ViMo's superiority as 'the first' visual GUI world model.

The GUI-text predictor pipeline requires multiple sequential LLM calls (identify unchanged symbols, assign semantic roles, predict text content) per prediction, adding latency (~30s) and multiple potential failure points; combined with STR diffusion generation, total inference is ~2 minutes for a single decision step involving 3 candidate actions, which seems difficult to reconcile with claims of practicality for real-time agent deployment.

The claimed relative-improvement percentages (e.g., 29.14%, 182.74%, 14.07%, 7.76%) are computed on very small absolute differences and small sample sizes in several tables, which can make relative-percentage framing appear more impressive than the underlying evidence supports.

Overclaiming in framing ("the first Visual world Model") when the core contribution is largely an application-level combination of existing techniques (diffusion-based layout editing + OCR + LLM text-infill) to a new domain, rather than a fundamentally new visual world-modeling approach.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: generating visual (not just textual) future GUI observations for App agent world models, filling a clear gap versus prior text-only world models.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is a simple but effective idea that decouples graphic layout generation (diffusion) from text content generation (LLM), directly targeting the known failure mode of pixel-level text rendering in diffusion models.

Comprehensive evaluation spanning three complementary settings: standalone world-model quality (automatic metrics + user study), agent-enhanced decision-making across 6 different App agents (language- and multimodal-based), and real-world applicability (zero-shot generalization to unseen apps, online navigation on AndroidWorld).

Reasonably strong and relevant baselines were constructed/adapted (IP2P fine-tuned on the GUI dataset, UI-diffuser, HTML-vision, Change-text/HTML-text language world models), giving a fair comparison across modalities.

Thorough ablations (static text preservation, action instruction vs. command conditioning, rollout iteration count) and supplementary analyses (randomness/variance study, trajectory synthesis error accumulation, inference time/practicality) that support the design choices.

Consistent, non-trivial gains are reported across agents and settings (e.g., step accuracy improvements for T3A/M3A, task completion rate gains in online navigation), suggesting the benefit is not an artifact of a single setup.
weaknesses: The overall system is an engineering pipeline stacking several existing components (OCR, a fine-tuned InstructPix2Pix-style diffusion model, multiple sequential LLM calls for filtering/semantic role/text prediction), which limits the technical/algorithmic novelty beyond the STR representation idea itself.

Evaluation relies substantially on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) for automatic metrics (sia, sar) and even for constructing/filtering the dataset and static text detection, raising concerns about circularity and potential bias favoring LLM-friendly outputs.

Dataset and test scale are fairly small (19 apps, 3,550 episodes; only 57 sampled episodes used for the main reported experiments), and although full-split results are claimed to be in the Appendix, the main paper does not report them, limiting confidence in statistical robustness.

The pipeline has notable latency (~2 minutes per multi-action request) despite claims of being "lightweight" and "plug-and-play," which could be a practical bottleneck not fully addressed for real-time deployment scenarios.

Failure cases (Fig. 6) show that text symbol detection/representation can break down, and the heuristic-based text overlay (color/font-size selection) may not generalize robustly to complex or stylized UI text elements.
The user study, while informative, only covers 80 samples across 4 methods, and details on inter-rater agreement or statistical significance of the reported differences are not discussed.

Baselines compared for pure GUI generation (IP2P, UI-diffuser) were not originally designed for this exact next-GUI-prediction task, and while fine-tuning (IP2P*) helps fairness, stronger/more specialized recent text-aware image generation baselines are not explored.
